newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Most East European markets climb to new highs.
newsitem.headline: Most East European markets climb to new highs.

text.p: Almost all East European stock markets staged strong performances this week, with Budapest, Prague, Warsaw and Ljubljana climbing to highs mostly due to foreign interest or good company results.
Two independent indices climbed to year highs in Bucharest in heavy trading and shares were mixed in Zagreb. Bratislava fought low liquidity, while Tirana had no trades.
The CESI Central European Share Index rose by 5.35 percent on the week to 1,713.63 points.
PRAGUE
The Czech PX50 soared to a year high on Thursday led by strong gains to the index's two most heavily capitalised shares, SPT Telecom and power utility CEZ.
In the week to Thursday, the PX50 rose 33.8 points, or 6.1 percent, to 591.3 but dealers cautioned against reading too much into the gains which they said had been partly made on low volume trading.
Dealers said they did not see any fundamental reasons for SPT shares to rise much further, but that CEZ could climb another two or three percent.
WARSAW
Polish shares rose this week to a 34-month high on Thursday and analysts expected a record on Friday.
The main market's WIG index rose 5.0 percent this week to 16,914.2 on Thursday.

Some analysts said the bourse, though fairly priced with an average price-earnings ratio of about 16, still had upside potential as Poland's economic prospects were good and firms' earnings this year were expected to grow at a fast pace.
They said the current growth might have been spurred by the recent release of company earnings in the fourth quarter and all of 1996, with some firms revising up earlier 1996 reports.
BUDAPEST
Hungarian shares continued the bull run this week, bolstered by domestic corporate news and predictions that the U.S. Fed would leave its rates steady.
But Wednesday saw early signs of profit-taking, which continued on Thursday, lowering the BUX index to 5,757.82 points, down from an all-time peak on Wednesday.
Traders said it was too early to say whether Thursday's fall or profit-taking on Wednesday were a correction before new rallies or the beginning of a reverse trend.
BRATISLAVA

Bratislava saw one more week of low volumes, but brokers said the highly undervalued market was starting to show signs of stronger foreign demand, which could put the bourse on a long-term uptrend in the near future.
The 16-share SAX index ranged between 186.21 points at Monday's open and 186.33 at Wednesday close, to rise 1.71 percent, or 3.19 points to 189.40 on Thursday.
Brokers said the market still needed a wider range of issues to boost liquidity.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares jumped 4.89 percent this week amid strong foreign demand. The 10-share SBI index soared 77 points to an all-time high of 1,650.58.
Market total turnover was 3.6 billion tolars.
Drug maker Lek's A issue was the biggest gainer, up 21.2 percent, while UBK bank led decliners, falling 8.8 percent.
BUCHAREST
Trading stayed lively in Bucharest this week, pushing turnover 10 million lei up on Thursday to 816.3 million and pushing two independent indices to year highs.

Bourse attraction Azomures closed the week 2,700 lei higher at 29,900, but brokers said buy notes amassed in the market for weeks were behind that rise rather than news of Azomures's privatisation after the sale of a 51 percent stake.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks were mixed throughout the week, with hoteliers forging ahead and blue chips pausing for a breath.
Analysts said all liquid issues were poised for mild gains amid growing foreign investor interest.
Trade was quite buoyant on Thursday following a stagnation that plagued the market earlier in the week.
TIRANA
The Albanian market, shaken by a crisis after the collapse of several pyramid investment schemes, saw no trading this week.
"Unfortunately, there were no transactions either on Thursday or on Monday," a dealer said.
